explanations.answer: Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The writer says, “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God…” (1 John 5:1). Look at what's missing from that sentence. No secret handshake, no membership card, no punch card with ten stamps. It's belief in Jesus, and that's the door.

explanations.answer: Everyone who keeps the law of Moses
explanations.explanation: Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is a big name, so I get why it came to mind. But the writer doesn't say a word about the law of Moses here. He says, “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God…” (1 John 5:1). Believing is the line he draws, not a checklist.

explanations.answer: Everyone who saw Jesus with their own eyes
explanations.explanation: Eyes are great, friend. I use mine to check the ovens every five minutes. But the writer doesn't say being born of God depends on seeing anybody. He says, “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God…” (1 John 5:1). It's about believing.

explanations.answer: When we love God and keep His commandments
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. The writer says, “By this we know that we love the children of God: when we love God and keep His commandments.” (1 John 5:2). Think about it this way. If I told you I love my ovens and then never turned one on, you'd squint at me. The love and the keeping go together.

explanations.answer: When we never argue with one another
explanations.explanation: A quiet kitchen sounds nice, friend. But that's not the test the writer gives. He says we know by this: “when we love God and keep His commandments.” (1 John 5:2). If never arguing were the test, I'd be in trouble before the first batch, because me and my oven timer go at it every morning.

explanations.answer: When we give away all we own
explanations.explanation: That one sounds serious, baker, but it's not what verse 2 says. The writer says the sign is, “when we love God and keep His commandments.” (1 John 5:2). Nothing about emptying your house. Besides, if I gave away everything I own, I'd be handing over a very tall chef's hat.

Careful, friend, this one is flipped around. The writer says the opposite: “And His commandments are not burdensome…” (1 John 5:3). Burdensome means heavy, like hauling a giant tub of dough up a flight of stairs. He says it isn't like that.
Right, baker. The writer says, “And His commandments are not burdensome…” (1 John 5:3). Not burdensome means they aren't a heavy load to haul around. He's saying they don't weigh you down.

explanations.answer: Everyone born of God overcomes the world
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Watch the little word that opens verse 4, “because.” The writer says the commandments aren't burdensome “…because everyone born of God overcomes the world.” (1 John 5:4). I think the point is that a load feels different depending on who's carrying it, and someone born of God has already overcome the world, so what God asks doesn't crush them.

explanations.answer: Everyone born of God is free from every trial
explanations.explanation: I'd love that one, friend, but it's not what the text says. The writer says everyone born of God overcomes the world, and overcoming is different from never facing anything hard. Jesus told His disciples they will have trouble in this world (John 16:33). So the verse is about overcoming, not skipping the trouble.

explanations.answer: Everyone born of God already knows them by heart
explanations.explanation: Knowing something by heart is handy. I know my recipe by heart and I still burn a batch now and then. But the writer doesn't give that as the reason. He says the commandments aren't burdensome “…because everyone born of God overcomes the world.” (1 John 5:4).

Yes, baker. The writer says, “And this is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith.” (1 John 5:4). Notice what the victory is. It's not a muscle or a trophy or a fancy title. It's our faith.

I can lift a full cookie box with my mustache, friend, so I like strength. But that's not the word in the verse. The writer says, “And this is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith.” (1 John 5:4). The victory isn't about how strong we are.
Wisdom sounds like a good guess, baker. But the writer doesn't name it here. Verse 4 says, “And this is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith.” The word is faith.

That's right, baker. The writer asks who overcomes the world, then answers: “Only he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God.” (1 John 5:5). Notice the question comes right after he calls our faith the victory in verse 4. So the one who overcomes is the one who believes.

It sounds almost too simple, so I'd double check too, friend. But it's right there in verse 5: “Only he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God.” (1 John 5:5). The writer says that's who overcomes the world, so this statement is true.
You got it, baker. The writer says Jesus Christ came “…not by water alone, but by water and blood.” (1 John 5:6). He's careful to say both. Water and blood, side by side.
Fire would make my ovens very happy, friend. But the writer doesn't say fire here. He says Jesus Christ came “…not by water alone, but by water and blood.” (1 John 5:6). The other one is blood.

Wind would just rearrange my cookie sheets, baker. The writer doesn't mention it in this verse. He says Jesus Christ came “…not by water alone, but by water and blood.” (1 John 5:6). So the answer is blood.

That's right, baker. The writer says, “And it is the Spirit who testifies to this, because the Spirit is the truth.” (1 John 5:6). He even says why the Spirit's word can be trusted. The Spirit is the truth.

It's a natural guess, friend. But the writer doesn't name the apostles as the ones who testify here. He says, “And it is the Spirit who testifies to this, because the Spirit is the truth.” (1 John 5:6). The witness he names is the Spirit.

A roomful of elders would be a fine crowd to have around my bakery, baker. But the writer doesn't name them in this verse. He says, “And it is the Spirit who testifies to this, because the Spirit is the truth.” (1 John 5:6). So the answer is the Spirit.

Yes, baker. The writer says the Spirit, the water and the blood are three that testify, “…and these three are in agreement.” (1 John 5:8). You know how you ask three friends for directions and get three different routes? Not here. The three line up.
Not this time, friend. The writer says the opposite: “…and these three are in agreement.” (1 John 5:8). No arguing at this table. The three testify together.

That's right, baker. The writer says, “Even if we accept human testimony, the testimony of God is greater.” (1 John 5:9). People's word can count for something, and God's testimony is greater still. He goes on to say what that testimony is.
That would be a tie, friend, and the writer doesn't call it a tie. He says, “Even if we accept human testimony, the testimony of God is greater.” (1 John 5:9). Greater is the word he picks.

The writer says the reverse, baker. He says, “Even if we accept human testimony, the testimony of God is greater.” (1 John 5:9). Greater, not harder to trust. In the very next verse he says whoever does not believe God has made Him out to be a liar (1 John 5:10).

Yes, baker. The writer says whoever “…does not believe God has made Him out to be a liar…” (1 John 5:10). That's a strong word, and he means it plainly. He ties it to not believing the testimony God has given about His Son.

Stranger sounds softer, friend, but it's not the word in the verse. The writer says whoever “…does not believe God has made Him out to be a liar…” (1 John 5:10). It's a heavy word, so I think this verse is worth reading slowly.

I see why you'd think of judge, baker, but that's not what the writer says. He says whoever “…does not believe God has made Him out to be a liar…” (1 John 5:10). The word is liar, and it comes from not believing the testimony God has given about His Son.

That's the one, baker. The writer says, “And this is that testimony: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son.” (1 John 5:11). Eternal life is what God has given us. Hang onto that one.

Riches would buy me a bigger mixer, friend, but that's not what the testimony says. The writer says, “And this is that testimony: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son.” (1 John 5:11). The gift is eternal life.

I live on a whole cookie planet and it's cozy, baker, but that's my story, not this verse. The writer says, “And this is that testimony: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son.” (1 John 5:11). The gift he names is eternal life.
Yes, baker. The writer says, “God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son.” (1 John 5:11). Then verse 12 goes on to say, “Whoever has the Son has life…” The life is found in the Son.
The temple is a good guess, friend, but it's not in this verse. The writer says, “God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son.” (1 John 5:11). The life is in the Son.
The law is a big word in the Bible, baker, but verse 11 doesn't use it that way. The writer says, “God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son.” (1 John 5:11). So the blank is Son.

I know, friend, this one is easy to get turned around. The writer says the opposite: “whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.” (1 John 5:12). It's a heavy line, so I think it's worth reading slowly. He puts it right beside the good news, that whoever has the Son has life.

That's right, baker. The writer says, “Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.” (1 John 5:12). It's a heavy line, and I think it's meant to be read slowly. No loopholes in either half of that verse.
